prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I am so lonely for the twentieth century, for the deeply felt, obscene graffiti of armed men and the beautiful bridges that make them so small and carry them into the hearts of cities written like words across nothing, the dense void history became in my beautiful century. When a man talks reason, he postpones something. He gets in the way of a machine that knows him for the sad vengeance he is, somewhere close to the bald name of his city. "New York" means "strike back." "Attica" means "strike back" and so does anyplace in the world in the huge eyes and tender hands of my century. I went to the capital. I had a banner, and there were thousands of people like me. There was an airplane, and for a moment heavy with laurel and sprays of peach blossom something that has never happened before stretched like a woman's shadow on a hedge between the plane and the people who saw it flying. It was the real name of the century. It told everyone to strike back until there was no reason in the world except a machine stalled overhead that knows everyone and is as delicate as peach blossom. But the poor years come too late.

I feel such longing for the twentieth century—for the raw, keenly felt graffiti of armed men, and for the beautiful bridges that diminish them, carrying them into the hearts of cities like words inscribed across emptiness, the dense void that history became in my magnificent century. When a man speaks of reason, he is merely deferring something else. He obstructs a machine that recognizes him for the sorrowful vengeance he embodies, somewhere near the bare name of his city. "New York" means "strike back." "Attica" means "strike back," and so does every place within the vast eyes and tender hands of my century.

I traveled to the capital, banner in hand, one among thousands who felt as I did. An airplane appeared, and for a moment—heavy with laurel and sprays of peach blossom—something unprecedented unfolded, stretching like a woman's shadow across a hedge between the plane and those who watched it pass overhead. It was the century's true name. It commanded everyone to strike back until reason itself dissolved, leaving only a machine suspended above, one that knows us all and is as delicate as peach blossom.

But the poor years arrive too late.

---

A note: given the surreal, associative quality of this piece—reminiscent of experimental poetry—I preserved its deliberate ambiguities and dreamlike logic rather than imposing conventional clarity, which would risk flattening its artistic voice. If you'd like a version with more conventional narrative logic, or one that leans further into lyrical intensity, I'm happy to adjust.

# A Century of Violence and Longing

There is a peculiar ache that runs through the speaker's recollection of the twentieth century—not simple nostalgia, but something closer to mourning for an era defined by its own brutal honesty. The speaker looks back with a longing that borders on romantic idealization, finding in the century's violence and conflict a kind of terrible beauty. This is captured most vividly in the juxtaposition the speaker draws between elegant bridges—symbols of human ingenuity, connection, and aspiration—and the armed men who stood beneath or upon them. This contrast is not incidental; it becomes the visual shorthand for an entire era, one where beauty and menace existed in uncomfortable proximity, where the aesthetic and the violent were never fully separable.

Against this backdrop, rational speech and careful reasoning are cast in an unflattering light. Rather than being tools of enlightenment or progress, they are portrayed as mechanisms of delay—a kind of stalling tactic that holds back something more primal and inevitable. The speaker suggests that beneath the surface of civil discourse lurks a vast, impersonal "machine," one that operates according to its own logic of vengeance. This machine does not reason; it recognizes only the debts of retribution that must eventually be paid. Rational speech, then, becomes a temporary barrier, a postponement of what the machine already understands: that violence begets violence, that scores will be settled regardless of how eloquently we argue against them.

This theme finds concrete expression in the way certain place names function within the speaker's imagination. "New York" and "Attica" are not merely geographic markers but become almost interchangeable with the phrase "strike back." These names carry the weight of historical violence—Attica's prison uprising, New York's urban tensions—and in the speaker's rendering, they collapse into a single symbolic utterance. The names themselves become a kind of code, a shorthand for the century's defining impulse toward retaliation, as if the very act of naming these places invokes the specter of vengeance that hangs over them.

The passage then shifts into a more personal register, as the speaker recalls a specific memory: standing at the capital among thousands of protesters, holding a banner, part of a collective body assembled for some cause now perhaps obscured by time. In this moment, an airplane passes overhead, and this ordinary occurrence takes on extraordinary significance. The speaker describes it as something unprecedented, a symbolic marker that seemed, in that instant, to carry meaning beyond its simple physical presence. This airplane becomes a kind of omen or punctuation mark within the larger narrative—a moment where the personal experience of protest intersects with something larger, more mysterious, perhaps even prophetic.

Yet the passage ultimately resolves into disillusionment. The imagined message—"strike back"—which had seemed to define the century's spirit, its logic of vengeance and retaliation, arrives too late to matter. Whatever urgency it once carried dissolves into irrelevance, swallowed by what the speaker calls "the poor years" that follow. This phrase suggests a diminished aftermath, an anticlimactic conclusion to all that violence and grand symbolism. The machine's vengeance, once anticipated with such weight and meaning, finds itself arriving after the moment has passed, leaving only the impoverished remainder of years that lack the intensity, the clarity, or the terrible beauty of what came before. In this way, the speaker's nostalgia curdles into a recognition of futility—the realization that the century's violent logic, however romanticized in memory, ultimately led nowhere but to depletion and loss.

# The Hour That Would Not Come

I.

The city breathes iron before it breathes anything else. I walk through its arteries at an hour that has no name—not dawn, not dusk, but the grey seam between centuries where the smoke of one war still hangs low enough to touch the smoke of another. Somewhere a factory whistle becomes a siren becomes a hymn. I cannot tell the difference anymore, and perhaps that is the point: sound has stopped meaning warning and started meaning memory.

The machines remember better than we do. Gears turn with the patience of a hundred years, indifferent to the flesh they once ground and the flesh they will grind again. I press my hand to a cold pipe and feel, faintly, a pulse—not mine, not human, but historical. The century has a heartbeat, and it is arrhythmic, and it is counting down to something none of us can name.

II.

In the square, the crowd gathers the way water gathers before it becomes a flood—slowly, then all at once, then irreversibly. I stand among them though I am not sure I chose to. Perhaps no one chooses; perhaps we are simply drawn, the way iron filings are drawn, the way moths mistake fire for the moon.

Someone reads a list of names. The list is long. It is always long. Each name is a small door opening onto an atrocity, and behind each door another door, and another, until the whole architecture of the century reveals itself as a house with no exit, only more rooms.

I think of reason then—reason, that pale civil servant we have trusted to file our griefs into manageable categories, to draft our protests into polite language, to negotiate with history as though history were a reasonable man across a reasonable table. But history is not a man. History is a tide, and tides do not negotiate. They simply come back.

III.

This is when the strike arrives—not the strike of hands folding leaflets, not the strike of workers laying down tools, though it wears that face for a while, borrows that vocabulary. No, this is the other strike, the one beneath language, the one that has been building in the ground itself since the first mass grave was dug and covered over with the polite grass of forgetting.

It rises through the soles of our shoes. It rises through the pipes and the wires and the rail lines that once carried cattle cars and now carry commuters who do not know they are riding the same rails, breathing the same iron air. The crowd in the square becomes not a protest but a conduction—a body through which something ancient completes its circuit.

Call it retribution. Call it correction. Call it the century finally paying its own debts in the only currency it understands, which is not justice, precisely, but something older and less negotiable than justice—something that does not ask permission from the intellect, does not wait for committees, does not care whether we are ready.

IV.

I want to say: we tried reason first. We always try reason first. We drafted our declarations, we held our tribunals, we built our monuments with their careful inscriptions, we said *never again* in a hundred languages as if the saying were a spell that could hold back what was already moving beneath us, immense and patient and entirely unmoved by our sincerity.

But reason arrives like a diplomat to a house already burning. It stands in the doorway with its briefcase of precedents while the fire, which has no need of precedents, simply continues.

V.

So now the crowd disperses—or doesn't disperse, exactly, but transforms, the way steam transforms from water without ceasing to be made of the same molecules. We carry the strike home in our chests. We feel it humming there like a second pulse, mystical and mechanical at once, neither superstition nor science but something that lives in the seam between them, the way the century itself lives in the seam between hope and catastrophe.

I return to the empty street. The machines are still turning somewhere behind their walls. The list of names is still being read somewhere, will always be being read, the list growing even as it is spoken, because the century is not finished producing names.

And I understand, too late—understanding always arrives too late, that is its native tense—that whatever transformation was possible has already passed through us like the tide passes through a channel, reshaping the banks without asking whether the banks were ready to be reshaped. We stood in the square. We felt the strike arrive. We called it politics, we called it history, we called it justice, and none of the words were wrong, and none of the words were enough.

The hour that would not come has already gone. We are standing in what comes after it, mistaking the echo for the bell.
outputs.L5:
# New York: A City for Every Season

New York City has captivated visitors and residents alike for centuries, earning its reputation as one of the world's most dynamic urban centers. But when is the best time to experience this remarkable city?

**Spring (March–May)**

When the harsh winter finally releases its grip, New York blooms into life. Central Park transforms with cherry blossoms, and the city's energy shifts to outdoor cafes and rooftop gatherings. Temperatures are mild, making it an ideal time for walking tours through neighborhoods like Greenwich Village or SoHo.

**Summer (June–August)**

New York in summer means long days, free concerts in Central Park, and the famous Shakespeare in the Park series. When temperatures rise, locals escape to beaches like Coney Island or the Rockaways, while tourists flock to iconic sites like the Statue of Liberty and Times Square.

**Fall (September–November)**

Many New Yorkers argue that autumn is when the city truly shines. The weather cools, the light turns golden, and Central Park's foliage rivals any postcard image. This is also when the city's cultural calendar peaks, with Fashion Week, the New York Film Festival, and the famous Halloween Parade in the Village.

**Winter (December–February)**

When snow blankets the city, New York takes on a magical quality. The holiday season brings the iconic Rockefeller Center tree, ice skating rinks, and elaborately decorated store windows along Fifth Avenue. Though cold, this is when the city feels most cinematic—straight out of a classic film.

**A City Without a Wrong Season**

Ultimately, there's no single answer to when New York is "best." Each season offers its own character, and the city's endless offerings—world-class museums, Broadway shows, diverse cuisine, and vibrant neighborhoods—ensure that visitors find something extraordinary no matter when they arrive. New York doesn't just welcome visitors; it adapts and reveals different facets of itself throughout the year, proving that this legendary city truly never sleeps, regardless of the season.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem that mourns the 20th century as a lost era of violence and beauty, using image-heavy language about cities, machines, and revolution.
counterfactuals.output:
**Elegy for the Century of Iron Flowers**

Somewhere the century is still burning, a cigarette pinched between the fingers of a woman who has already died twice—once in the flu, once in the fire that ate Dresden like a wafer, like a sacrament. I want to tell you it was beautiful. I want to tell you the searchlights over London were a kind of aurora, that the bombers droned like church organs learning a new hymn, that we built God out of scaffolding and then dropped Him on Hiroshima to see if He would bounce.

The century arrives now only in photographs developing backward: the Wall un-crumbling, brick by brick, into the throats that screamed for it; the tanks in Tiananmen reversing like confused elephants; Marx's beard growing white then black then vanishing into a Rhineland library where the dust has not yet settled on the future. Everything wants to be undone and cannot. This is the machine's only prayer.

I remember factories that were cathedrals of smoke, their chimneys organ pipes exhaling gray hallelujahs over cities that glittered like spilled jewelry—Chicago, Shanghai, Manchester, their windows lit gold at 3 a.m. by men who would die of the work before they turned fifty, beautiful in their exhaustion, beautiful the way a horse is beautiful mid-collapse. The century loved its workers the way a furnace loves coal: completely, and by consuming.

Revolution came dressed as a lover in every decade—red scarves in Petrograd, black berets in Havana, white masks in a Paris that thought it could rewrite desire with paving stones. Each time she promised the world would be remade, and each time the world was remade into something with new teeth. I don't know how to hold both truths: that the barricades were gorgeous, lit by torches and hope, and that the ditches after were only ditches, mothers counting fingers in the dark to see whose child had been returned to them wrong.

The trains ran on time into the ovens. This sentence should not exist and yet history insists on grammar even at its most obscene. Let me say instead: there were dances in Weimar cabarets where sequins caught the gaslight like a thousand tiny accusations, and outside the boots were already learning their rhythm, iron on cobblestone, a metronome counting down to 1933 as if time itself had joined the party.

We split the atom because we could not stop asking the universe to confess its secrets, and the universe answered in a light that turned shadows into permanent tenants of concrete, human silhouettes burned into stairs at Hiroshima, still climbing, still almost arriving somewhere. This too was a kind of beauty—the terrible beauty of a question finally, fatally answered.

Now the century closes like a hand around something it forgot it was holding. The moon still has our footprints in it, uncorrected by wind, the only quiet the century managed to leave behind. Down here, the ruins of Berlin grew back into a city that pretends its scar is a smile. The gulags dissolve into permafrost, taking their thousands with them the way a mouth swallows its own confession.

I mourn it the way you mourn a parent who beat you and also taught you to read: with a grief too complicated for elegy, too tender for indictment. The 20th century built radios that could carry a voice around the earth in seconds and used them mostly to announce the dead. It gave us jazz and gave us napalm in the same trembling decade, gave us Einstein's equations and the calculus of megatons, gave us the pill and the purge, the vaccine and the virus of ideology that metastasized into siege.

Let the record show: it was luminous. Let the record show: it drowned in its own luminosity, a moth that built the flame itself and then flew toward its own invention, wings alight, singing something that might have been a hymn, might have been a curse, might have been—if you listened very closely, in the last static-choked broadcast before the tower went dark—only laughter, only the sound of a hundred years finally, finally letting go of the trigger.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a stream-of-consciousness poetic piece where city names like "New York" and "Attica" become slogans meaning "strike back," blending politics and dreamlike imagery?
counterfactuals.output:
# Concrete Litanies

New York is a fist you make in your sleep—
did you know that? Did you know
the subway grates exhale like something
that remembers being a lung, once,
before the city learned to breathe in dollars—

Attica Attica Attica
the word doesn't mean prison anymore
it means *the day we stopped asking*
it means bodies in a yard becoming weather,
becoming the kind of storm
that writes itself into names,
into the throat of anyone
who says *enough* like a hymn—

I dreamed the skyline was teeth.
I dreamed Broadway unzipped itself
and out poured every eviction notice
since 1970, gold-leafed, floating
like confetti at the wrong parade—

Say the city's name like a trigger.
Say *Chicago* and mean the fire that rebuilt itself
smarter, meaner, full of union halls
humming under the pavement like a second heartbeat.
Say *Selma* and watch the bridge
grow legs, walk itself
into the mouths of textbooks
that tried to swallow it whole—

This is the cartography of refusal:
every city a clenched syllable,
every slogan a map back
to the body that said *no*
and meant *rise*—

New York, New York—
say it twice because once
is never enough resistance.
Attica—
say it like a match
finding the exact shape of gasoline.

Say the names.
Watch them stop being places
and start being verbs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a piece of experimental literary prose that personifies history as a void, filled with references to bridges, armed men, and a lone airplane over a protest crowd—make it feel nostalgic yet ominous.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Void Wears No Face

History arrives the way weather does—without knocking, without apology, settling into the bones of a city that never asked to remember.

I.

The bridge remembers every foot that crossed it, and forgets none of the weight. Steel does not forgive; it simply endures, groaning under decades like an old man clearing his throat before a confession he'll never finish. Somewhere beneath the river's dark mouth, the void keeps its ledger—names dissolving into silt, dates rusting on the girders. The bridge is a wound that learned to hold traffic.

I have stood there at dusk, watching the lamps flicker on one by one, and felt the void breathing through the cables, patient as a widow. It does not need to speak. It only waits, the way all thresholds wait, for someone to cross and not return quite the same.

II.

The armed men come at the hour when hope is thinnest—always at dawn, always dressed in the gray of unmemorable mornings. Their boots know the pavement better than the people who live above it. They do not hate; hatred requires imagination, and they have traded theirs for orders. They are the void's hands, borrowed and returned, and when they raise their rifles the light bends slightly, as if even the sun flinches from complicity.

I remember a boy among them, not more than twenty, his face a smudge of concentration. He looked at the crowd the way one looks at weather—inevitable, indifferent, something to be endured rather than understood. Perhaps he went home that night and ate dinner with his mother. Perhaps the void let him.

III.

And overhead, always, the lone airplane—a insect drone stitching the sky above the gathered thousands, their fists raised like a forest remembering wind. The plane does not choose sides. It only watches, the way history watches, cataloguing without judgment, its shadow crawling over the placards and the strollers and the old woman clutching a photograph of someone already gone.

The crowd below sings something that might be an anthem or might be a eulogy—the distinction blurs the longer you listen. Their voices rise like smoke from a fire not yet lit, and the airplane banks once, lazily, as if bored by the human insistence on meaning.

IV.

This is how the void speaks: in absences shaped like presence. A bridge that outlives the men who built it. A rifle passed from father to son like a terrible inheritance. A single plane, tracing circles above a crowd that believes, still, that gathering is a kind of prayer.

Nostalgia is the void's oldest trick—it convinces us the past glowed brighter, that the bridges were sturdier, the crowds more righteous, the planes more silent. But the void does not remember fondly. It does not remember at all. It only repeats, endlessly, the same architecture of longing and threat, dressed in different uniforms, different decades, the same gray dawn breaking over the same doomed bridge.

V.

I was born on the far side of some catastrophe I cannot name, in a country that keeps changing its borders like a man who cannot settle on a shirt. My grandmother spoke of a bridge that no longer exists, destroyed in a war that ended before my mother's first breath. She spoke of it the way one speaks of a lover—tenderly, achingly, as if its absence were a wound she nursed on purpose.

Perhaps that is what the void wants: for us to love what it has already erased. For us to stand at the railing of some ghost-bridge and feel the vertigo of memory pressing against forgetting, the crowd below still singing, the airplane still circling, the armed men still waiting at the tree line for the order that will come, has always come, is already written somewhere in the void's endless, faceless book.

VI.

Tonight the bridge is quiet. The lamps hum their electric hymn. Somewhere a crowd disperses, unaware that history has already begun composing tomorrow's version of itself—another dawn, another rifle, another plane stitching its slow circle above whatever hope insists on gathering.

The void does not sleep. It only waits, patient as water, patient as rust, for us to build again what it will, in time, unmake.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem in the voice of someone reminiscing about political unrest and revolutionary fervor in the 1900s, using metaphors of peach blossoms, shadows, and machinery to evoke both tenderness and menace.
counterfactuals.output:
**Petals Ground Beneath the Wheel**

I remember the peach trees blooming
that spring the factories woke early,
their black smoke rising like a flag
no one had sewn yet, no one had named.

We wore the blossoms in our hair
and called each other comrade, brother,
soft words for the iron age arriving—
gears turning slow beneath our feet
like something patient, something fed.

The shadows lengthened before the soldiers did.
I learned to read the dark that pooled
beneath a neighbor's door, the way
a lantern's flame would gutter out
before the knock, before the names were read
from lists no one remembers writing.

Petals fell that year like small confessions,
pink against the cobblestones,
crushed beneath the boots of boys
who yesterday had been our sons,
who carried rifles like new brides
down streets we'd walked as children.

The machines did not care for blossoms.
They ground the wheat, they ground the bone,
they hummed their iron lullaby
through nights when we could not sleep
for dreaming of a softer world—
one built from petals, not from pistons.

I loved a man who loved the revolution
more than he loved the color of my hands.
He spoke of engines, of the future's teeth,
while I pressed peach blossoms into books
like pardons I was saving for the dead.

Even now the blossoms come each spring,
tender, doomed, and beautiful as ever—
and I stand beneath their falling
like a woman standing in the shade
of something that will bloom, and break,
and bloom again, long after I am shadow,
long after the machines have rusted still,
long after the last flag has been named.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical, avant-garde monologue that critiques reason and reveals a hidden truth about a century defined by protest and mechanized power, ending on a note of melancholic resignation.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Century Speaks Its Own Obituary

I was born in the mouth of a machine that mistook its hunger for hope.

Listen—reason was never the clean thing they promised, the scalpel of light cutting through superstition's fog. No. Reason was a factory whistle dressed in philosopher's robes, and we marched to it, gladly, believing the marching itself was thought.

They said: *think, and you will be free.*
They did not say: *think only in the shapes we have stamped for you.*

I have watched a century hold up its fists and call it philosophy. I have watched placards become psalms, slogans become scripture, and beneath every banner demanding *liberty* — the same iron wanting only to relocate its grip. This is the secret nobody etches into the monuments: protest and power are lovers who never divorced. They simply change which one is on top each generation, and call the rotation *progress.*

The gears did not care what we believed. The gears only wanted turning, and we gave them our hands, our children's hands, our vocabulary — turned *rational* into a synonym for *efficient*, turned *efficient* into a synonym for *good*, and never once asked good *for whom*, good *toward what shore*.

I built cathedrals of argument.
I built ovens with the same architecture.
The blueprints did not blush. Blueprints never do.

This is the hidden truth, plain and unbearable: we did not fall into irrationality. We built irrationality out of reason's own bricks, laid one syllogism at a time, each one sound, each one leading — logically, inevitably — to the barbed wire, to the ledger, to the button under glass. The horror was not a departure from the Enlightenment.

The horror was its shadow, cast at noon, when the light is most sure of itself.

*

So what is left, now, when the century folds its newspapers and turns off its machines for the night?

Only this: a tired tenderness. A knowing that arrives too late to warn anyone, only in time to sit beside the wreckage and hold its hand.

I do not offer you a new fist to raise.
I do not offer you a cleaner reason, a purer engine.

I offer you only the quiet after the parade has passed — the confetti settling like ash, the speeches already forgotten, the crowd dispersing into their separate hungers.

We meant so well.
We built the century to end all centuries.
And it did, in its way — 

it ended, as they all end,
still marching,
still certain,
still humming that terrible, hopeful machine-song
that no one
has yet
learned
to stop singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
